title: Juniper and the Lost Bunny
markdown:
In the heart of the Misty Crags, where clouds nested around the hills like scarves, Juniper kept a house that smelled of sweet herbs and warm honey. She was a young witch whose magic liked making things cheerful: hearths that held, windows that welcomed. One late afternoon she was dusting sparkle onto the glass so it would look like stars when a whimper found the doorstep, small as a sigh.

She opened the door a crack. On the stone sat the smallest, fluffiest bunny she had ever seen. Ears drooped. Pink nose twitched. The whole of him trembled as if the evening had arrived too quickly.

“Oh, you poor little thing,” Juniper whispered, and made her smile as warm as a cookie still on the tin. “Come inside.”

He hopped in with a wiggle of tail. She decided he looked like a Pipkin, and the name settled as if it had been waiting in the chamomile. The hearth glowed. Round windows watched like sleepy eyes. She poured a saucer of garden-herb milk that smelled wonderfully soothing. He drank, whiskers quivering, then let out another small whimper that made Juniper’s heart ache a little.

“My name is Juniper,” she said, voice like a gentle song. “You seem to have lost your way.” Pipkin only wiggled his nose. She smiled a soft, reassuring smile. “Don’t worry. We will find your home. The moon is only peeking over the mountains, like a shy pearl. There is time before dark. Your family will be waiting.” She put on her woolliest cloak, twilight-coloured. Pipkin, a little braver beside her, hopped out, ears lifting a fraction to the pine-hum of the path, needles brushing the twilight air.

They had not gone far when they found an old wizard on a smooth stone, beard a mix of white and grey with ink in it, maps spread around him like a quilt. Forests, ribbon-rivers, star-charts, and places that might have been only dreams. Professor Marmalade looked up as if lostness were a hobby he respected.

“Hullo there. Lost, are we? Or looking for a happy shortcut?”

Juniper explained. Pipkin was lost. Bedtime was coming. Family would be waiting. The Professor’s eyes brightened. He murmured over maps: Whispering Waterfall, Sleepy Willow grove, a wiggly route, a place famous for moon-berries. He unfurled a sheet so large it nearly covered the clearing. Lines tangled like a playful worm.

Juniper admired it. She also saw the truth under Pipkin’s feet. “It’s a lovely map,” she said, “but it makes the journey twisty and long. His home is just over the gentle slope, where the blue primroses grow.” She pointed toward the setting sun.

Professor Marmalade blinked, then laughed, a rumble that seemed to sway the leaves. “Much simpler than this suggests. Sometimes the most direct path is the one under our noses, or a little way over the hill. Follow the dew-kissed clover. You’ll be there in no time.” He folded the clever sheet without sulking. “A wiggly line can lead somewhere wonderful. A straight one is what you need when you are going home.”

They took the slope. Clover sweetened the air with a meadowy perfume that whispered of warmth. The path was ordinary grass and a line of quiet pines, nothing a cartographer would boast about, and Pipkin’s ears stayed pointed toward it as if maps were a language he had never needed. Ancient trees gathered like friendly shoulders. Soon, near a cluster of them, came the sounds: happy chirps, soft squeaks, hope with whiskers.

In a dry hollow beneath an oak whose roots made welcoming arms, a rabbit family waited with ears perked and noses twitching. Pipkin’s mother, fluffy, kind-eyed, rushed forward at once, nuzzling him with relief. “Oh, Pipkin! We were so worried. We looked everywhere.” Pipkin, done with whimpering, nudged her and then hopped to Juniper and licked her slipper, a small grateful punctuation.

His father bowed his whiskers. “Thank you. You are a very kind young witch, and we are glad you found our Pipkin.”

Juniper felt sunshine bloom in her chest and did not turn it into a lesson. “It was my pleasure,” she whispered above the rustling leaves. She waved. The last sun painted lavender and rose. Pines sang a lullaby on the walk back. The first shy stars pricked the velvety sky.

In her house she made a mug of honey-sweetened tea, steam rising in gentle swirls, and took the armchair that was as soft as a cloud. The moon sat like a silvery smile, casting peaceful shadows that danced like sleepy fireflies. She closed her eyes on the last of the steam, warm and content, and the Misty Crags, which had not needed a wiggly map after all, lulled her as gently as the slope had lulled a bunny home.
